chunks: Ali ibn Abd Allah al-Warraq (mercy of Allah be upon him) said: Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn Buttah said: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Mahbub, and Muhammad ibn al-Husayn ibn Abd al-Aziz narrated, on the authority of Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, on the authority of al-Husayn ibn Sa'id, on the authority of Hammad ibn Isa al-Juhani, on the authority of Hariz ibn Abd Allah, on the authority of Abu Abd Allah (peace be upon him), who said:

Verily, people regarding divine decree (al-Qadar) are of three types: One man claims that Allah, the Mighty and High, compelled people to commit sins; this man has wronged Allah in His judgment, so he is an unbeliever. And one man claims that the matter has been delegated to them (absolute delegation); this man has weakened Allah in His sovereignty, so he is an unbeliever. And one man claims that Allah obligated the servants with what they can bear and did not obligate them with what they cannot bear; when he does good, he praises Allah, and when he does evil, he seeks forgiveness from Allah; this is a complete Muslim.

key_terms.مُفَوَّضٌ: Delegated or handed over (doctrine of Tafwid)
key_terms.يَطِيقُونَ: What they can bear or have capacity for

ai.seo_question: What are the three views on divine decree in Shia theology and which is considered correct?
ai.summary: This hadith from Shaykh al-Saduq’s *al-Tawhid* refutes the extremes of Jabriyyah (divine compulsion) and Mu'tazilah’s Tafwid (absolute delegation) to establish the Shia doctrine of *Amr bayn al-Amrayn*. It emphasizes that true faith lies in recognizing Allah’s justice by commanding only what humans can bear, thereby preserving both divine sovereignty and human agency.
